input:
It is also worth noting that the Chilton-Colburn analogy extends essentially the same relation to mass transfer, with $j_D$ taking the place of the heat-transfer factor. Under this analogy, $j_D$ is equal to $f/2$, which means that the mass-transfer factor is exactly one half of the friction factor for the same flow. This relation is based on the assumption that the boundary layers for momentum and for the transferred component develop in essentially the same way, thereby allowing a single coefficient ratio to describe both processes in a unified manner.

A brief numerical check helps to illustrate the typical size of the numbers involved. For turbulent flow in a smooth pipe at a Reynolds number of 20000, the measured value of $f$ is 0.0064. Applying the analogy then gives $j_D = f/2 = 0.0032$. If a measured mass-transfer coefficient converts to a value of $j_D$ that is well away from 0.0032, this is generally taken, under the analogy, as an indication that one of its underlying conditions is not fully satisfied in the flow under consideration, and the check is used in precisely that direction: agreement supports the measurement, whereas disagreement directs the reader back to the conditions rather than to the arithmetic.

However, the qualification is arguably just as important as the relation itself. Friction in a pipe consists of two components: skin friction at the wall and form drag, which arises where the flow separates or changes direction. The boundary-layer argument that underpins the analogy covers skin friction only. In situations where form drag accounts for a large share of $f$, such as flow across a bank of tubes or through a packed bed, $f$ increases without any matching increase in the transfer rate, and $j_D$ correspondingly falls below $f/2$. As a result, the analogy then overstates the transfer factor, and the magnitude of the error grows in line with the form-drag share. Nevertheless, within its conditions — namely turbulent flow, dominant skin friction, and similar behaviour of the two boundary layers — the relation remains a compact and useful way to estimate a transfer factor from a friction measurement, as well as to check a measured transfer factor against the friction of the same flow.
